title: The Arnolfini Portrait
hook: Someone else is in this room.
caption:
Someone else is in this room. Look in the mirror.

Jan van Eyck painted a merchant and his wife in Bruges in 1434, then hid two visitors in a convex mirror no bigger than your palm. One wears red. Above it, he wrote on the wall like graffiti: "Jan van Eyck was here."

One lit candle in daylight. Oranges worth a fortune. Kicked-off shoes. And no, she's not pregnant.

Swipe to read the room, then watch the reel and step inside the painting yourself. Save this for your next National Gallery visit.

slides.headline: The Arnolfini Portrait
slides.alt: The whole painting in a gold frame: a man in a black hat and fur cloak holds the hand of a woman in a green gown in a Bruges bedroom.

slides.headline: A merchant, and a mystery.
slides.alt: Side-by-side crops of the man's pale face under his huge hat and the woman's face under a white linen headdress.

slides.headline: She's not pregnant.
slides.alt: Torn paper scrap showing the woman gathering up the folds of her green fur-lined gown in front of her waist.

slides.headline: So why is one candle lit?
slides.alt: The brass chandelier with a single lit candle, circled in gold, the other holders empty.

slides.headline: Every object whispers.
slides.alt: Three tall crops: oranges on the windowsill and chest, wooden pattens on the floorboards, and the small shaggy dog.

slides.headline: Two visitors in the doorway.
slides.alt: Small view of the painting with a gold ring on the mirror, leading to a large circular zoom showing the couple from behind and two figures in blue and red in the doorway.

slides.headline: Bruges to London.
slides.alt: Timeline: 1434 painted in Bruges, 1516 Margaret of Austria, 1558 Philip II, 1813 leaves Spain, 1842 bought by the National Gallery for 600 guineas.

slides.headline: "Jan van Eyck was here."
slides.alt: The Latin signature 'Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434' above two paper scraps: the visitors in the mirror and Van Eyck's Man in a Red Turban.

notes: Hedged: man in red = Van Eyck (NG asks it as a question); Man in a Red Turban as self-portrait (traditional, unproven); candle-as-memorial is Margaret Koster's theory; 1813 Vitoria/Joseph Bonaparte route unconfirmed, so slide says 'a British officer turns up with it'. Infrared claim follows Billinge & Campbell 1995 abstract (faces, hands, feet). Not used: the Passion roundel sides (only the count of ten is on slide 7), her red slippers.
